title: Rabindranath Tagore

cards.b:
Rabindranath Tagore (1861-1941) was a poet, educator and thinker, and in 1913 the first non-European Nobel laureate in literature (for Gitanjali). In politics he was an internationalist and a critic of aggressive nationalism, a stand that makes him vital to Paper I.

He translated Gitanjali himself from Bengali into English, and the 1912 London edition, with an introduction by W.B. Yeats, brought him Western fame.

In lectures given in Japan and the US in 1916-17 and published as Nationalism (1917), Tagore described the nation as an organised political and commercial power, a machine that crushes human values and breeds aggression and race hatred. He condemned the West's imperial nationalism and warned India not to imitate it.

He said India's real problem is social, not political: caste and communal divides.

Tagore called Gandhi 'Mahatma' and admired him, but they debated. On non-cooperation (1920-21) he feared a negative, narrow spirit and burning of foreign cloth as wasteful. On the charkha, in The Cult of the Charkha (1925), he said that spinning cannot be the way to swaraj, and called for free thought. Gandhi answered in 'The Poet and the Charkha'. The 1934 Bihar earthquake exchange: Gandhi called it divine punishment for untouchability, Tagore rejected the idea.

In Swadeshi Samaj (1904) Tagore urged that Indians build self-reliant society independent of the state, through village cooperation, schools and local work. He founded the rural institute at Sriniketan (1922) near Santiniketan to test this with cooperatives and village crafts and health work.

Tagore founded Visva-Bharati University at Santiniketan in 1921 as a meeting place of world cultures. It is an institutional example of his belief that education should connect the village and the world.

Tagore disliked rote schooling as 'a cage'. In 1901 he opened a school at Santiniketan with classes under trees, and in 1921 Visva-Bharati, 'where the world makes a home in a single nest'. He stressed creativity, the arts, nature and the meeting of cultures. Visva-Bharati became a central university in 1951.

• Some nationalists felt he was detached from the freedom struggle.
  • His own Ghare Baire (1916) shows nationalism's moral risks, but he supported Swadeshi in 1905.
  • Critics say his stress on society ignored the need to win power from the British.
  • In 1919 he gave up his knighthood to protest Jallianwala Bagh, proof of his political courage.

Compare: Gandhi (village, moral action), Nehru (liked Tagore's internationalism and modernity), Vivekananda (spiritual nationalism). Tagore sits closer to a cosmopolitan liberal humanism. His song Jana Gana Mana became India's national anthem, Amar Shonar Bangla Bangladesh's.

His 1917 book Nationalism, based on lectures given in Japan and the United States, warned that nationalism had become a political and economic organisation that could threaten other peoples.

His warnings echo in current debates on aggressive nationalism, citizenship and cultural identity. The poem 'Where the mind is without fear' (Gitanjali) is a favourite essay quotation. Santiniketan was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2023.

His 1930 Hibbert Lectures, published as The Religion of Man (1931), argued for a humanism beyond any single creed. That speaks to present debates on religion and public life.

Structure: Nationalism 1917, Gandhi debates, Swadeshi Samaj, education, critique, relevance.

A strong answer can cite his 1917 Nationalism lectures, his 1921 letter to Gandhi on non-cooperation, and his 1919 renunciation of knighthood after Jallianwala Bagh.

His last major statement, the 1941 address 'Crisis in Civilisation', is worth citing on the limits of Western progress.
